SUMMARY_FINDINGS: **Card sort findings.** Three Weber State students sorted the 20 cards: two did an open sort and one did a closed sort to check the categories. All three put 6 pairs of cards together every time: search with seats, degree progress with prerequisites, add with submit, weekly schedule with overlap checking, paying with the tuition rules, and advisor with the glossary. The biggest split was over class days and times. The freshman treated them as part of searching, while both seniors treated them as part of planning a schedule.
METHOD_PARTICIPANTS:
**Participants.** Three Weber State students with a range of registration experience took part on November 6, 2026.

| ID | Year | Times registered at Weber State | Sort type | Format |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P1 | Freshman | 2 | Open | Remote, text message |
| P2 | Senior | 5 to 6 | Open | Remote, text message |
| P3 | Senior | 7 | Closed | Remote, text message |

**Procedure.** P1 and P2 got the same written instructions and the 20 cards as a numbered list. They sorted the cards into groups that made sense to them, named each group as if it were a menu label, put anything that didn't fit in an "Unsure" group, and said which card was hardest to place.

P3 did a **closed sort**. They got the same cards plus 6 category names drawn from P1 and P2's labels (Find Classes, Register, My Schedule, My Degree, Finances, Help) and a "None of these" option. This is a standard way to check whether categories that came out of an open sort make sense to someone who didn't create them.

Remote sorting by text let participants work on their own schedule without the facilitator in the room. Raw replies and session notes are in `01_card_sort/raw_data`.

**Limitations.** Three participants is the minimum, so the agreement percentages show a direction, not a statistically reliable result. Combining open and closed sorts in one similarity matrix is common for hybrid studies, but P3 could only choose among the given categories. Their sort tests the categories rather than inventing new ones. Two of the three participants are seniors, so newer students are underrepresented.
RESULTS:
**Groups created.** P1, the freshman, made 7 narrow, descriptive groups (for example "Course Search & Exploration" and "Registration & Account Information"). P2, a senior, made 4 broad, one word groups: "register," "schedule," "degree," and "finances." P3 used all 6 provided categories and did not use "None of these." No participant used an Unsure pile.

**Common categorization patterns**

* **Degree and prerequisites belong together, and apart from registration.** All three participants grouped them identically. Today, prerequisite checking lives in CatTracks, which Phase 1 found students open in a separate tab. Students expect it in one place called "degree."
* **Money is its own space.** All three paired the tuition and drop rules with paying, not with registering. That supports a Finances section. It also helps explain Phase 1 finding HE03: students don't look for the drop rule while they are registering, so the redesign repeats it next to the Register button.
* **Add and submit are one action.** All three grouped them together, so the redesign keeps the path from Add to Register short, with a "Review and register" link on every Find Classes page.
* **Advisor and glossary are both "help."** All three paired C19 with C20, which supports putting them side by side in the utility nav.

**Label disagreements**

* **"Registration" means two different things.** P1 split it into Enrollment & Registration (doing it) and Registration & Account Information (checking status). P2 used one word, "register," for almost everything. The redesign follows P1's split: doing happens in Find Classes and My Schedule, and checking status happens on Registration Home.
* **Holds (C16)** went to finances for 2 of 3 participants and account information for 1. Holds appear on Registration Home, because a hold blocks registration, and are also listed under Finances.
* **Choose a semester (C14)** landed in a different group for every participant. With no agreed home, it becomes a global header switcher reachable from every page instead of a step inside one section.
* **Drop a class (C10)** went to register for 2 of 3 and schedule for 1. Drop lives in My Schedule's Registered table, next to the Register button.

**Unexpected mental models**

* **Seniors see class times as schedule planning, not search.** Both seniors put "See what days and times a class meets" with schedule, while the freshman put it with search. An experienced student isn't asking "what sections exist?" but "which section fits my week?" The redesign keeps a live week view in the My Schedule sidebar on the Find Classes page and flags conflicts on each result before Add.
* **Experience shrinks the menu.** The freshman needed 7 categories, but the most experienced open sorter needed only 4. Five primary nav items sits between them. That's enough to keep degree and finances separate, which everyone wanted, without the fine split only the newer student made.
* **The hardest cards were the "obvious" ones.** P1 found the glossary (C20) hardest, and P3 found degree progress (C07) hardest. Yet every participant put those cards in the same group. Hesitating doesn't mean a card has no clear home. These are tasks students rarely think about during registration, which supports showing them in context (an inline CRN definition and prerequisite status on each result) instead of only in their own section.

**How the data tested the draft IA**

I sketched a draft sitemap from the Phase 1 findings before running the sort, then checked each decision against the data.

| Draft decision | What the sort showed | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary item "Tuition and Billing" | The open sorters named this group "finances," and P3 confirmed it | **Changed:** renamed to Finances |
| Holds shown only on Registration Home | 2 of 3 put holds with finances | **Changed:** holds stay on Home and are also listed under Finances |
| My Degree as its own primary item | 100% agreement from all three participants | **Confirmed** |
| Week view sidebar and conflict flags on Find Classes | Both seniors grouped times and section comparison with schedule | **Confirmed and promoted:** treated as a core part of Find Classes, not a convenience |
| Semester as a global header switcher | No two participants agreed on where it belongs | **Confirmed** |
| Advisor and glossary in utility nav | 100% agreement | **Confirmed** |
| Join waitlist on each full section in Find Classes | P3 placed the waitlist under Find Classes | **Confirmed** |
| Registering actions split between Find Classes (Add), My Schedule (Submit, Drop), and Home (registration date) | Add, submit, drop, and registration date form a 72% cluster | **Open issue** for Phase 3 (below) |

**Open issue for Phase 3.** The data shows students think of "register" as one place, but my IA spreads registering across three pages. I kept the split because each action sits where its context is: Add next to the section, and Submit next to the pending list and drop rule. The pending count badge and "Review and register" links tie them together. Phase 3 usability testing should check whether students find the Register button without help, and whether a nav label such as "Schedule and Register" works better than "My Schedule."
REFLECTION_1:
Going in, I assumed students think about registration the way the system is built, as a set of tools: a search tool, a schedule, a degree audit, and a billing page. Before running the sort, I sketched a draft sitemap based on the Phase 1 findings. It had "Find Classes" as the search area, a schedule sidebar beside the results mostly as a convenience, and a primary item called "Tuition and Billing."

The data supported the big pieces but challenged the details. All three participants pulled degree progress and prerequisites into their own group, and all three made a finances group. That confirmed that CatTracks being a separate app is a structural problem, not just a visual one.

The biggest surprise was how experience changed people's mental models. Both seniors put "see what days and times a class meets" under **schedule**, not under searching, while the freshman put it with search. I had treated time as a search attribute. Experienced students treat it as a planning question: which section fits my week. That changed how I see my own design. The week view sidebar on Find Classes is not an extra. It answers the question students are actually asking, so it stays on that page, and the conflict flags on each section are essential, not optional.

The labels challenged me too. Nobody said "billing." The open sorters said "finances," so I renamed the nav item. I had also expected "registration" to be one clear category. P1 split it into doing (enrolling) and checking (account information), while P2 used "register" for almost everything. "Choose a semester" landed in three different groups for three people, which convinced me it shouldn't live inside any one section.

The data also exposed something I don't think I fully solved. Students see "register" as one place, but my design spreads adding, submitting, and dropping across pages so each action sits next to its context. I kept that decision on purpose, but it's the first thing I want to test in Phase 3.

Finally, the difference between a freshman making 7 groups and a senior making 4 showed me there's no single "correct" number of categories. The right structure has to work for both. Five flat items with no sub-menus was a better compromise than my instinct to add more specific sections.
